questions.q: What does the spilled range operator, e.g. A2#, actually mean in a formula?
options: Whatever the spilled array starting at A2 currently contains, resizing automatically if that spill grows or shrinks
A hardcoded reference to the exact range A2 originally spilled into, that never updates
A syntax error in older versions of Excel
It multiplies A2 by the number of rows in the sheet
questions.explain: The # operator always refers to the current spill, however large it is right now — unlike a hardcoded range like A2:A11, it can never fall out of sync with the spill's actual size.

questions.q: Why is =SUM(A2#) generally better than =SUM(A2:A11) when A2 holds a dynamic array formula?
options: A2# automatically tracks the spill's current size, while A2:A11 becomes wrong the moment the spill grows or shrinks
There is no difference between the two
A2:A11 is faster to calculate
A2# only works with text values, not numbers
questions.explain: A hardcoded range like A2:A11 is only correct for the spill's size at the moment you wrote it — the spill operator stays correct as the source data changes.

options: Excel calculated a dynamic array's result but couldn't place it because something is occupying a cell in its intended spill area
The formula contains a typo in a function name
The workbook has run out of available worksheets
The formula successfully spilled and this is just an informational note
questions.explain: #SPILL! specifically means the result was calculated but blocked from landing — most often by existing data sitting in the spill's path.

questions.q: Which of these will prevent a dynamic array formula from spilling at all, regardless of blank cells around it?
options: Placing the formula inside an Excel Table, or having a merged cell in its path
Using a longer formula name
Placing the formula in row 1 of the worksheet
Using more than one dynamic array function in the same workbook
questions.explain: Excel Tables don't support spilling at all, and dynamic arrays cannot spill through merged cells — both block the spill structurally, not just by occupying a cell.

questions.q: What's the fastest way to find exactly what's blocking a #SPILL! error?
options: Click the error indicator on the cell and choose Select Obstructing Cells
Delete the entire worksheet and start over
Manually check every cell on the sheet one at a time
Restart Excel
questions.explain: The error indicator's Select Obstructing Cells command jumps straight to whatever is sitting in the spill's intended path.
